Notes: C#- OOP-II

OOP-II
​​​​​​​Inheritance, polymorphism, and hiding are fundamental concepts in object-oriented programming (OOP) in .NET. Each of these concepts plays a crucial role in how classes interact with one another and how behavior can be extended or overridden in derived classes.
Inheritance
  1. Inheritance is the capability of a class to use the properties and methods of another class while adding its own functionality. 
  2. Enables you to add new features and functionality to an existing class without modifying the existing class.
  3. Base class and Subclass  
  4. A Baseclass or parent class is the one from which another class inherits attributes and behavior.
  5. A subclass or child class is a class that inherits attributes and behavior from a Baseclass.

​

Types Of Inheritance

Constructor hierarchy
​​​​​​​Order of constructors calling with inheritance

  1. With non-static constructors
In case of inheritance if we create an object of child class then the parent class constructor will be called before child class constructor. i.e. The constructor calling order will be top to bottom.
Example:
    class Person
    {
        public Person() {
            Console.WriteLine("In Person Constructor");
        }
    }
    class Student:Person { 
        public Student() { 
            Console.WriteLine("In Student Constructor");
        }
    }

    class Program
    {
        static void Main(string[] args)
        {
            Student student = new Student();
        }
    }
Output:
In Person Constructor
In Student Constructor

With static constructors
In the case of a static constructor, calling order will be reversed from non-static i.e. it will call from bottom to top.

Example:
class Person
    {
         static Person() {
            Console.WriteLine("In Person Constructor");
        }
    }
    class Student:Person {
        static Student() { 
            Console.WriteLine("In Student Constructor");
        }
    }

    class Program
    {
        static void Main(string[] args)
        {
            Student student = new Student();
        }
    }
Output:
In Student Constructor
In Person Constructor

In C#, you can call the parent class constructor by using the "base" keyword, followed by the constructor's parameters in parentheses. For example, if the parent class has a constructor that takes in two integers as arguments, you would call it in the child class constructor using "base(int1, int2)".

For example:
class Parent
{
    public Parent(int x, int y)
    {
        // constructor implementation
    }
}

class Child : Parent
{
    public Child(int x, int y, int z) : base(x, y)
    {
        // constructor implementation
    }
}
In this example, the Child class constructor is calling the parent class constructor using the base keyword and passing x and y as arguments.

Polymorphism
​​​​​​​Polymorphism is a Greek word that means multiple forms or shapes. 
You can use polymorphism if you want to have multiple forms of one or more methods of a class with the same name.
In C#, polymorphism can be achieved in two ways:
1. Compile-time Polymorphism (Method Overloading)
2. Run-time Polymorphism


​​​​​​​
Method Overloading 
  Compile-Time (Method Overloading)
  1. Compile-time polymorphism is also known as method overloading. C# allows us to define more than one method with the same name but with different signatures. This is called method overloading.
  2. Method overloading is also known as early binding or static binding because which method to call is decided at compile time, early than the runtime.

​​​​​​Rules for Method Overloading:
  1. Method names should be the same but method signatures must be different. Either the number of parameters, type of parameters, or order of parameters must be different.
  2. The return type of the methods does not play any role in the method overloading.
  3. Optional Parameters take precedence over implicit type conversion when deciding which method definition to bind.

Example :
public class OverloadExample
{
    // Method with the same name but different parameters (method overloading)
    public int Add(int a, int b)
    {
        return a + b;
    }

    public double Add(double a, double b)
    {
        return a + b;
    }

    public string Add(string a, string b)
    {
        return a + b;
    }
}
class Program
{
    static void Main()
    {
        OverloadExample example = new OverloadExample();

        // Calling the overloaded methods
        int sumIntegers = example.Add(5, 10);
        double sumDoubles = example.Add(3.5, 2.5);
        string concatenatedStrings = example.Add("Hello, ", "world!");

        Console.WriteLine($"Sum of integers: {sumIntegers}");
        Console.WriteLine($"Sum of doubles: {sumDoubles}");
        Console.WriteLine($"Concatenated strings: {concatenatedStrings}");
    }
}
Output:
Sum of integers: 15
Sum of doubles: 6
Concatenated strings: Hello, world!
Method Overriding
​​​​​​​Runtime Polymorphism: Method Overriding
  1. Run-time polymorphism is also known as inheritance-based polymorphism or method overriding.
  2. Inheritance allows you to inherit a base class into a derived class and all the public members of the base class automatically become members of the derived class. 
  3. However, you can redefine the base class's member in the derived class to provide a different implementation than the base class. This is called method overriding that also known as runtime polymorphism.
  4. In C#, by default, all the members of a class are sealed and cannot be redefined in the derived class. Use the virtual keyword with a member of the base class to make it overridable, and use the override keyword in the derived class to indicate that this member of the base class is being redefined in the derived class.

Example:
  class Person
    {
        public virtual void Greet()
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Hi , I am Person");
        }
    }
    class Employee : Person
    {
        public override void Greet()
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Hi , I am Employee");
        }
    }

    class Program
    {
        static void Main(string[] args)
        {
            Person p = new Person();
            p.Greet();

            Person p2 = new Employee();
            p2.Greet();

            Employee emp = new Employee();
            emp.Greet();
        }
    }
Output:
Hi , I am Person
Hi , I am Employee
Hi , I am Employee

  Note:
 If you remove override keyword from derive class method, It will call Parent class method.
Output will be:
Hi , I am Person
Hi , I am Person
Hi , I am Employee

Rules of Overriding:
  1. A method, property, indexer, or event can be overridden in the derived class.
  2. Static methods cannot be overridden.
  3. Must use virtual keyword in the base class methods to indicate that the methods can be overridden.
  4. Must use the override keyword in the derived class to override the base class method.

In C#, you can call a method from the parent class in a child class by using the "base" keyword, followed by the method name and its parameters in parentheses. For example, if the parent class has a method called "Method1" that takes in no arguments, you would call it in the child class using "base.Method1()".

For example:
class Parent
{
    public void Method1()
    {
        // method implementation
    }
}

class Child : Parent
{
    public void Method2()
    {
        base.Method1();
    }
}
In this example, the Method2 in the Child class is calling the Method1 from the parent class using the base keyword.

Alternatively, you could also use the override keyword to redefine the method in the child class and call the method using base.Method() within the child class method.
Hiding, using new
​​​​​​​Use the new keyword in the derived class to hide the base class method. This will be useful when you are reusing third-party APIs where you don't have control over the base class.

Example:
class Person
    {
        public virtual void Greet()
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Hi , I am Person");
        }
    }
    class Employee : Person
    {
        public new void Greet()
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Hi , I am Employee");
        }
    }

    class Program
    {
        static void Main(string[] args)
        {
            Person p = new Person();
            p.Greet();

            Person p2 = new Employee();
            p2.Greet();

            Employee emp = new Employee();
            emp.Greet();
        }
    }
Output:
Hi , I am Person
Hi , I am Person
Hi , I am Employee

Difference between hiding and overriding
  1. The "override" modifier extends the base class method, and the "new" modifier hides it.
  2. The "virtual" keyword modifies a method, property, indexer, or event declared in the base class and allows it to be overridden in the derived class.
  3. The "override" keyword extends or modifies a virtual/abstract method, property, indexer, or event of the base class into the derived class.
  4. The "new" keyword is used to hide a method, property, indexer, or event of the base class into the derived class.
  5. If a method is not overriding the derived method then it is hiding it. A hiding method must be declared using the new keyword.
  6. Shadowing is another commonly used term for hiding. The C# specification only uses "hiding" but either is acceptable. Shadowing is a VB concept.
  7. For hiding the base class method from derived class simply declare the derived class method with the new keyword.
  8. Whereas in C#, for overriding the base class method in a derived class, you need to declare the base class method as virtual and the derived class method as overriden.
  9. If a method is simply hidden then the implementation to call is based on the compile-time type of the argument "this".
  10. Whereas if a method is overridden then the implementation to be called is based on the run-time type of the argument "this".
  11. New is reference-type specific, overriding is object-type specific.
